description: Misfit group of medical students born to yap and forced to chart. Fuelled by caffeine, fear of OSCEs, and ambition to advance patient care in space.
summary:
Mindmap is a clinical system designed to monitor and support crew mental health on long missions. It builds a personal baseline for each crew member from vital signs, cognitive function, movement, and clinically validated questionnaires collected at regular intervals. Deviations from baseline are flagged for follow-up, and the system screens for medical and environmental causes that could mimic psychiatric conditions, such as elevated cabin carbon dioxide or monoxide, illness, medication side effects, and sleep disruption.

When a change is detected, the system notifies the astronaut, with optional on-board medical officer intervention, and sends the flight surgeon a ready-made consult summary to help develop a care plan. The aim is to detect prodromal symptoms of behavioural and psychiatric disorders before they escalate to serious events such as psychotic episodes or suicide attempts.

Crewed missions to Mars cannot count on real-time support from Earth. Communication delays can last up to 22 minutes one way, and disruptions can last from several days to several months, so a flight surgeon cannot assess a crew member as events unfold. By detecting early warning signs and giving crews a structured plan for early intervention, our system bridges these delays and gives Earth-based teams the full picture as soon as they can respond.

Our solution is designed to add to NASA’s Behavioural Health and Performance work and can extend to remote and low-resource care on Earth.
details:
The Problem 

During long-distance space travel, crews are confined to tight quarters and experience extended periods of isolation. Crews travelling between Earth and Mars will be subject to these trying conditions for approximately seven months on each leg of the voyage. While rigorous pre-launch preparations could promote resilience to such conditions, the behavioural and mental deterioration of crew members cannot be reliably predicted, as recognized by the 2025 NASA Behavioural Medicine Evidence Report.

The average annual incidence of severe mental health and psychological disorders exceeds 60% in space flights exceeding 600 days. A 2023 review reports that NASA found symptoms of anxiety in 22.8% of male and 85.2% of female astronauts, and symptoms of depression in 34.8% of male and 43.2% of female astronauts. In-flight behavioural assessment and early intervention are thus essential to preventing acute psychiatric events and protecting astronauts’ health. 

Current strategies to support crew member mental health include daily journaling, virtual reality headsets for relaxation, and regular private conferences with flight surgeons. These approaches depend on timely two-way communication, which becomes limited as crewed missions extend deeper into space. On a Mars-bound mission, communication delays can reach 22 minutes each way, and disruptions can last from several days to several months. NASA’s Comm Delay Assessment found that delays increased individual stress and frustration and reduced task efficiency and teamwork. 

The latent gap in care is evident. Current mental health support is built around scheduled, real-time conversations with Earth, which will become increasingly compromised as communication delays grow. New systems are required to monitor crew members, interpret early changes against established indicators and thresholds, and guide initial care without explicit intervention from Earth. NASA recognized this in its June 2026 Human Research Program risk approach plan, which highlighted the need to “identify indicators, measures, and thresholds, to inform semi-autonomous behavioural health and performance monitoring.” 

Our Solution

Mindmap is a monitoring system designed to help astronauts catch early warning signals of deterioration in their mental health—including subclinical changes that fall below the threshold for diagnosis—so that they can act before these develop into conditions such as clinical depression or anxiety. It compares each astronaut with their unique baseline and flags concerning shifts in sleep, mood, energy, cognition, and physiology. When a pattern of changes resulting from primary psychiatric etiology is identified, Mindmap prompts the astronaut to follow up with the medical team and suggests strategies, such as CBT-based techniques, to capture the benefits of early intervention.

The system also prepares a structured clinical note for the astronaut’s health records that is accessible by their assigned flight surgeon. The flight surgeon can then use the included clinical history, trends, and screened secondary causes to develop a care plan, allowing better use of valuable appointment time. For higher-risk findings, the on-board medical officer is alerted right away with a recommended plan. The system informs and supports. Clinical decisions stay with the astronaut, the medical officer and the flight surgeon.

How it works

Mindmap consists of three core components: construction of a baseline profile for each crew member, in-flight monitoring of biopsychosocial health signals, and a flag-intervene-evaluate loop when risk factors for mental deterioration are identified.
Constructing a Baseline Profile:

In the months before the mission, a unique profile is constructed for each astronaut. Metrics of cognition, including concentration, verbal memory, attention, and spatial and mathematical reasoning, are measured across multiple sessions using NASA’s established WinSCAT battery. Concurrently, crew members complete extended evaluations with a psychologist. Rather than evaluating mental resilience and adaptability, these interviews seek to identify patterns of stress response that crew members are already aware of. Potential questions include: 

  • What types of situations and tasks increase your stress levels or make you feel drained?
  • What does stress feel like to you? What thoughts and feelings make you aware that you are under stress, or that your mental health may start to deteriorate?
  • Are there any coping strategies or activities that you know make you feel better in times of stress? What external sources of social support help you?
  • Do you find reminders to maintain your mental health useful? How can teammates and colleagues help keep you mentally healthy?

Additionally, these interviews will establish defined scales for mental distress which will be used during in-flight monitoring. For example, crew members could be asked:

  • What does 10/10 loneliness or stress feel like to you? What about 7/10, 5/10, or 3/10? What experiences in your life align with this scale that you can compare to? 

Crew members will also collaborate with the psychologists to develop guidelines for what information they want shared automatically with the healthcare team, as well as plans to ensure crew safety in the event of a critical deterioration in their mental condition, such as active suicidal ideation or psychosis. Finally, crew members will be asked to complete 3-minute PVT, PHQ-9, GAD-7, and C-SSRS tests—clinically validated tools for monitoring cognitive fatigue, depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation, respectively. 

The collected psychological information will be combined with pre-flight monitoring of key biological measures including average sleep duration and regularity, time to sleep, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, and exercise response and recovery. Together, these data compose the biopsychosocial baseline profile of each crewmember. As the crew adapts to life onboard the spacecraft, the profiles will be updated using a rolling average of a 14-day window excluding days flagged as indicative of possible mental distress.

In-Flight Monitoring of Biopsychosocial Health Signals:

During the mission, psychological and physiological markers of crew member mental health will be monitored through a combination of automatic measurement and active reporting. These include metrics such as sleep duration, reaction speed, resting heart rate and variability, exercise response and recovery, body mass, blood pressure, blood temperature, and CO2 intake.

Astronauts complete a brief daily check-in rating their perceived stress, mood and fatigue, with an optional journal entry describing their thoughts and stressors. Once a week, they are prompted about other factors that affect mental health, such as loneliness or homesickness, team conflict, workload and time pressure, sleep-medication use, and changes in appetite or food fatigue. These weekly questions capture psychological factors that a daily rating can miss. Check-ins can become more frequent, with additional prompts, when a concerning pattern appears or when the astronaut wants closer monitoring. If a pattern points to low mood, anxiety or hopelessness, short validated screening questions are triggered, following the safety plan agreed before flight.

Flag-Intervene-Evaluate Loop:

Over the course of the voyage, health metrics will be flagged when they fall out of a crew member’s normal baseline range. These flags and signal trends are clearly visualized on the crew member’s dashboard to allow personal management of their health. Flags are presented as simple status changes rather than evaluative scores (ex: sleep scores), as receiving negative scores can worsen performance through the nocebo effect.

An increased risk of psychological deterioration is detected based on a concordance of flags across multiple signals. When a pattern is identified, the crew member is prompted to complete follow-up tests appropriate to the flags; for example, a pattern of increased stress and onset insomnia is consistent with anxiety disorders, and a GAD-7 test would be administered by the system. Mindmap simultaneously checks biological signals and cabin conditions to rule out non-psychiatric etiology. This is similar to current clinical practice of how physicians work through a differential diagnosis. Only tests which would change management are completed to reduce false positives and unnecessary interventions. Depending on the pattern of flags and results of the follow-up test, Mindmap may recommend that the crew member to involve the medical team. The system also prepares a structured clinical note for the flight surgeon to streamline pertinent information the flight surgeon would otherwise have to collect during limited care conferences. Critically, this note is not sent automatically, maintaining crew member control over their health data, patient confidentiality, and respect for their medical autonomy.

In addition to suggesting involving the health team, the system provides personal recommendations based on the biopsychosocial profile developed pre-flight. Crew members could be prompted to complete CBT resources, prioritize exercise, speak with other crew members, or contact family. Mindmap might also recommend a change in workload such as deferring tasks known to increase stress levels, minimizing shift changes, and increasing rest time. The crew member is prompted after the intervention to evaluate any changes in mood, helping guide further recommendations. They are also free to dismiss recommendations, resulting in them being suggested less often in the future. Any associated changes in biological signals are also used to select future interventions.

Two exceptional circumstances change the system’s response: triggering rules from the pre-established safety plan, and risks of severe deterioration threatening crew member or team safety. For example, in pre-mission preparation, the crew member could have set a rule that if a specific crewmate grew concerned for their health, then the flight surgeon would be automatically contacted and a clinical note sent. Similarly, the flight surgeon and on-board medical director would be automatically contacted if risks of suicidal intent or psychosis were detected. These conditions mirror those found in psychiatric mandatory reporting guidelines intended to keep patients safe.

Benefits

For Astronauts:

Each astronaut receives individualized feedback on their own health metrics, including trends in sleep, mood, energy, vitals, and cognitive function that are compared against their baseline. By distinguishing normal day-to-day fluctuations from clinically meaningful deviations and concerning trends, the system provides simple status indicators to help astronauts recognize when changes may warrant attention. Each alert includes a plain-language explanation of what has changed, why it may matter, and clinically proven strategies they can implement independently between check-ins. This empowers astronauts to better understand and manage their own health, while providing an avenue to seek support from the onboard medical officer and ensuring concerns can be reviewed during weekly private care conferences with the flight surgeon. Feedback is designed to inform and support rather than alarm, minimizing unnecessary worry and alert fatigue.

For the Medical Team:

The system generates structured clinical notes that capture pertinent information needed by medical teams to assess astronaut health, formulate differential diagnoses, and develop a care plan. The consult follows the SBAR format: the situation (what changed and the current risk level), the background (baseline, mission day, relevant history and medications), the assessment (which measures deviate and by how much, and which medical and environmental causes have been screened), and the recommendation (what the medical officer has been advised to do and what decision is requested). This process reduces information loss and improves care coordination when real-time communication with Earth is not possible.

What we hope to achieve

Primary aim: Shift in-flight mental health support from a reactive to proactive approach. Subclinical changes should be noticed and supported before they progress to clinical diagnoses with more serious health and career consequences, without relying on an immediate response from Earth.

  • Streamline Care: Make limited, delayed contact count, so flight surgeons spend it on decisions and care planning, including what to do if mental health worsens, not on history-taking.
  • Astronaut Autonomy: Equip astronauts to understand and manage their own mental health between contacts with Earth. Give them their own trends, self-management strategies, and clear guidance on when to involve the medical team, so they can act on early signs and not only report them.
  • Reduce Stigma: Lower barriers to speaking up in a high-performance career by treating mental health monitoring as a routine part of staying at peak performance, so seeking support is not read as a risk to flight status. 
  • Earth aim: Adapt the approach for rural and remote communities, where specialists are far away, and for high-stakes professions (for example, medicine or air traffic control), where delayed support can affect the safety of others, enabling earlier help and clearer communication with the care team.

Tools:

We used Claude to help us with the coding of the project. In Claude, we inputted the variables we wanted the system to assess including mental health surveys for anxiety and depression, vitals, ECG, etc. We also used Claude to help with making the slide theme for this project. The content was written by us. 

We also used Claude to refine our project plan, helping us improve writing coherence. No images or videos were made with SI generation.
